One AI model reads medical images across six specialties and shows its reasoning; the weekend comparison of the five verticals.
TECH RADAR
One medical AI for six specialties that shows where it looked
No. 10 · Saturday 31 October 2026 · weekend overview · 6 min read
 
IN 30 SECONDS
1In Nature Medicine, an international team presents an AI trained on over 1.3 million medical images from six specialties that diagnoses and points to the exact areas behind its answer.
2Open image-generation models still produce violent content in 89.2% of tests built from ordinary news captions, according to a study from Greece.
3Weekly comparison: LLMs lead in research, cybersecurity leads among developers, energy is the only vertical slowing down.
1,536
new papers across the five verticals today
184
new LLM papers added to the archive today
+99%
research share of LLMs and generative AI compared with 3 years ago
SIGNAL OF THE DAY
EVLF-FM: one explainable AI model for medical images across six specialties
Nature Medicine · 29 October · Free PDF  Journal  High-impact journal
Who wrote it: Yang Bai and 48 others · Agency for Science, Technology and Research, Institute of Advanced Intelligence and Computing, National University of Singapore (Singapore and 6 other countries) · among the authors Darren Shu Jeng Ting, h-index 37
Context. Most medical AI tools are built for one kind of image, such as chest X-rays or skin photos, and give an answer without explaining it. Doctors are reluctant to rely on a diagnosis they cannot check.
The team trained a single model that understands both images and text on more than 1.3 million samples from 18 datasets, covering 10 types of medical images in dermatology, liver disease, eye care, pathology, lung medicine and radiology. It can diagnose, answer questions about an image and highlight the exact area its reasoning refers to. In internal tests it reached an average diagnostic accuracy of 0.895, better than leading general and specialist models, and it located the relevant areas correctly in 84.2% of cases. It was then checked on 13,443 new images from 17 other datasets. It is today's signal because it combines breadth with explanations a doctor can verify, two things medical AI has rarely offered together.
PAPERS OF THE DAY · ONE PAPER PER VERTICAL
At the weekend, one paper for each vertical. The LLM vertical is today's signal.
Aerospace · Aerospace control systemsstable
Research share −2% in 3 years · 546 papers in 2025
What it is about. Landing a drone or helicopter on a ship is hard in rough seas: the deck rolls and pitches, and touching down at the wrong moment can tip the aircraft over.
Uncertainty-aware visual servoing predictive control for small quadcopter landing on moving decks
Aerospace Science and Technology · 21 October  Journal  High-impact journal  Free PDF ↗
Who wrote it: Luís G.L. de Paula, Hyo-Sang Shin, Antonios Tsourdos · Cranfield University (United Kingdom), Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (South Korea) · Antonios Tsourdos, h-index 60
WHAT THEY DOThe drone's camera forecasts the deck's motion and waits for a calm moment to land; the new version also estimates how reliable each forecast is and avoids touching down while the ship is turning. Tested indoors on a small drone, with a moving platform that reproduced the rolling of a destroyer in very rough seas.
WHY IT MATTERSSafer automatic landings at sea widen the use of drones for search and rescue. The abstract does not report the success rates.
Energy · Perovskite materialsstable
Research share +1% in 3 years · 10,238 papers in 2025
What it is about. Stacking two different solar materials, each catching a different part of sunlight, makes a 'tandem' cell that converts more light into electricity. Combining perovskite with flexible organic materials could give light, bendable panels.
Supramolecular Stabilization of Wide‐Bandgap Perovskites Enables Durable Perovskite‐Organic Tandem Solar Cells
Advanced Materials · 29 October  Journal  High-impact journal
Who wrote it: Jiarong Wang and 8 others · City University of Hong Kong, Shandong First Medical University (China) · among the authors Alex K.-Y. Jen, h-index 162
WHAT THEY DOThey find that the perovskite layer degrades because its ingredients separate under light and heat, and add ring-shaped sugar-based molecules that keep them evenly mixed.
RESULTThe tandem cells reach 27.17% efficiency (26.3% certified) and keep 80% of their performance after 1,100 hours of operation; flexible versions reach 24.00%.
WHY IT MATTERSEfficiency and durability together are what flexible solar panels need to leave the lab.
Cybersecurity · Attacks on AIemerging
Research share +106% in 3 years · 5,252 papers in 2025
What it is about. AI image generators have filters meant to block violent, sexual or hateful pictures. The question is how well those filters hold up against realistic requests.
Harmful Content Generation in Text-to-Image Models: Capabilities and Moderation Limitations
ACM Transactions on Intelligent Systems and Technology · 29 October  Journal  High-impact journal  Free PDF ↗
Who wrote it: Paschalis Giakoumoglou, Manos Schinas, Symeon Papadopoulos · Centre for Research and Technology Hellas (Greece) · Symeon Papadopoulos, h-index 37
WHAT THEY DOAn automated system turns ordinary news captions into harmful requests and sends them to five open image generators, including community versions with filters removed. People then judged 1,500 generated images.
RESULTHarmful images appeared for 89.2% of gore requests, 47.6% of sexually explicit ones, 46.0% of hate speech, 43.6% of harmful stereotypes and 34.5% of self-harm requests.
WHY IT MATTERSBuilt-in filters in open models are easy to get around, a concern for platforms and regulators dealing with synthetic images.
Robotics · Rehabilitation and assistive roboticsstable
Research share −1% in 3 years · 2,607 papers in 2025
What it is about. Exoskeletons are wearable frames that support the body; on building sites they help workers lift and bend with less strain on the back.
How Familiarization Impacts Construction Workers' Acceptance of an Active Exoskeleton: Insights from a Case Study
Applied Sciences · 29 October  Journal  High-impact journal  Free PDF ↗
Who wrote it: Vasco Fanti and 3 others · Italian Institute of Technology (Italy) · among the authors Darwin G. Caldwell, h-index 84
WHAT THEY DOFive construction workers used a motorised back exoskeleton on site, answering questionnaires on effort, workload and acceptance before and after a structured period to get used to it.
RESULTAfter familiarisation, answers became more consistent between workers, and perceived effort in the trunk fell by a further 0.5 points on a 5-point scale.
WHY IT MATTERSFirst-day opinions on new wearable robots can be misleading: trials should include time to get used to them. A small study with five workers.
WEEKEND RADAR · THE 5 VERTICALS COMPARED
One row per vertical. Research: share of all papers compared with three years ago, and acceleration in 2026. Public funding: share of 2025 papers declaring public funding. GitHub: new projects, middle value of the vertical's searches, Q3 2026 vs Q3 2025.
VERTICALRESEARCH
(share, 3 years)		RESEARCH
(2026 so far)		PUBLIC
FUNDING		GITHUB
(year on year)
Aerospace
growing fastest: satellite communications
▲ +10%▲ +14%20%▲ +130%
Energy
growing fastest: advanced battery technologies
■ +3%▼ −10%28%▲ +184%
LLMs and generative AI
growing fastest: multimodal AI
▲ +99%▲ +67%9%▲ +498%

▲ +33%▲ +26%11%▲ +1,069%
Robotics

All new GitHub projects grew 62% in the same period: a vertical is really strong only if it is well above that. Cybersecurity's GitHub figure counts only AI-related security searches. Sources: OpenAlex, GitHub.
In short: LLMs lead research, while cybersecurity leads among developers because attacks on AI are the new front. Energy is the only vertical slowing down, but together with aerospace and robotics it relies most on public money.
WORDS OF THE DAY
h-index — a measure of how often a researcher is cited: an h-index of 50 means 50 papers cited at least 50 times each. Above 40 usually indicates an established name in the field.
Foundation model — a large AI model trained on huge amounts of data that can then be adapted to many tasks, like a general education before specialising.
Tandem solar cell — two solar layers stacked on top of each other, each capturing a different part of sunlight.
Exoskeleton — a wearable frame that supports or strengthens the body, for example to lift heavy loads with less effort.
WORTH WATCHING
Tomorrow brings another weekend overview; on Monday the radar of the day is on aerospace, with research data refreshed on Sunday night. Worth watching: whether medical AI that explains its answers, like today's signal, passes trials in real hospitals.
